1.stem: How does the research described in Text 2 complicate Socrates's warning in Text 1?

options.A: It vindicates Socrates completely, showing that people who keep a written record remember less of everything, including where the record itself is kept.
options.B: It refutes Socrates by showing that keeping a written record leaves a person’s recall entirely unaffected.
options.C: It supports part of Socrates's warning (weaker recall of recorded specifics) while showing that memory is redirected rather than simply diminished.
options.D: It demonstrates that people in oral cultures — those without writing — remembered less than literate people who keep written records.

2.stem: Which finding, if true, would most support the alternative interpretation?

options.A: At the earliest plazas, construction proceeded in small, uneven increments consistent with many independent work parties rather than one directed effort.
options.B: The very largest plazas are found in precisely those cities that also contain the most elaborate royal tombs and the longest surviving lists of the names of kings.
options.C: Later plazas were frequently rebuilt on a grander scale by kings who recorded their own names on the stairways and monuments they added to the older spaces.
options.D: The pavements of the plazas required sophisticated engineering knowledge to drain rainwater from such large flat surfaces.

3.stem: Based on the passage, the heightened frontal activity in older adults is best understood as

options.A: a response to inefficiency in other brain regions rather than the direct source of memory ability.
options.B: a sign that older adults' memory performance must therefore exceed that of younger adults on the same tests.
options.C: proof that increased activation in a brain region is generally unrelated to task performance.
options.D: conclusive evidence that the frontal regions have taken over as the primary engine of memory in later life.

4.stem: Which choice is most strongly supported by the text?

options.A: Reducing visible disorder may fail to reduce crime when the community conditions underlying both are left unaddressed.
options.B: Visible disorder bears no relationship at all to the level of serious crime in a neighborhood, since the two arise from entirely separate conditions.
options.C: Serious crime is what produces the visible disorder found in disadvantaged neighborhoods, reversing the direction of cause the original theory proposed.
options.D: Removing visible signs of disorder such as graffiti and shattered glass is an effective way to prevent the serious crime that those signals invite.

5.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text with an inference?

options.A: The novelist chose the windowless corner because the view from the window distracted her from the page.
options.B: The novelist regarded revision, not initial drafting, as the stage that produced publishable work.
options.C: The novelist valued the rapid morning drafting at the window above the slow work of revision.
options.D: Nothing the novelist wrote at the window desk was worth keeping, which is why she reread those pages so rarely.

6.stem: Which choice is most strongly supported by the text?

options.A: Pastoral poems were the work of actual shepherds setting down the realities of country labor.
options.B: The pastoral's chief purpose was to attack the system of aristocratic patronage on which its own poets depended.
options.C: The pastoral offered aristocratic readers a genuine escape from patronage, ambition, and the court.
options.D: The pastoral's apparent rusticity served as a means of addressing sophisticated, courtly concerns indirectly.

7.stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

options.A: Anglerfish males are far smaller than females because, once fused to her body, they draw all their nutrients from her bloodstream.
options.B: Anglerfish reproduction is inefficient, since the male that attaches to a female degenerates until little of him remains but gonads.
options.C: The male anglerfish's permanent fusion to the female is an adaptation to the difficulty of finding mates in the deep sea.
options.D: Life in the deep sea, where sunlight never reaches and encounters between individuals are rare, forces most fish to live attached.

8.stem: Which finding would most weaken a stylometric attribution of a disputed passage to a collaborator?

options.A: The credited dramatist is well documented as having collaborated often over the course of his career.
options.B: The named collaborator is documented as having written portions of several other plays staged in that same decade.
options.C: Function words such as 'and' and 'the' are indeed hard for a writer to imitate on purpose.
options.D: The disputed passage is in a dramatic genre not represented among the credited author's comparison samples.

9.stem: Which choice best states an inference supported by the text?

options.A: Yellow blossoms yield more prey than white ones, which is why the spider settles on them.
options.B: The spider matches a new blossom the moment it settles on it, so switching flowers costs it no hunting time.
options.C: Camouflage matters less to ambush hunters than to web builders, since prey wanders close either way.
options.D: The spider's hunting success depends partly on how well its color currently matches its perch.

10.stem: Which finding, if true, would most WEAKEN the passage's position?

options.A: The dismantling mechanism was found to operate only during periods of sleep, pausing whenever the animals were awake.
options.B: Blocking the memory-dismantling neurons prevented essentially all forgetting in the animals tested.
options.C: Humans and animals were found to forget at markedly different rates.
options.D: Some memories faded even when the dismantling neurons remained fully active.

11.stem: Which finding would most directly support the geologist's argument?

options.A: The ash contained mineral grains identical to those in the surrounding lakebed sediment.
options.B: The ash layer was of even thickness across the whole lakebed, showing no thinning in any direction.
options.C: The ash was chemically similar to deposits found in several other regional lakes.
options.D: The ash layer was thickest near the point where a stream had once entered the lake.

12.stem: Which statement about the willow recovery is best supported by the passage?

options.A: The willows would have recovered to exactly the same extent even if wolves had never been reintroduced.
options.B: Drought and hunting were the primary drivers of willow recovery throughout the park.
options.C: Wolves reengineered the ecosystem by triggering the return of beavers and stable rivers.
options.D: Wolf predation was neither the sole nor the decisive cause of the willows' return.

13.stem: Which choice best captures the 'subtler revision' the passage proposes?

options.A: The unusual density of the region's wild cereals made monument-building unnecessary for the site's builders.
options.B: Agriculture and monument-building arose at the same time but developed independently of each other.
options.C: Monument-building may have been among the causes of agriculture rather than a result of it.
options.D: The site's builders had already domesticated wild cereals before they raised the enclosures.

14.stem: Which finding would most directly support the neuroscientist's proposal?

options.A: Birds that sang more phrases during the day spent more total time asleep.
options.B: Sleeping birds showed neural firing sequences matching those recorded during daytime singing.
options.C: Birds deprived of sleep for a single night sang their practiced phrases with noticeably more errors the following day.
options.D: Sleeping birds showed higher overall brain activity than birds that were awake.

15.stem: Which finding would most strengthen the "old friends" refinement over the original hygiene hypothesis?

options.A: Children who bathe less often have fewer allergies than children scrubbed daily from infancy.
options.B: Farm-raised children with broad animal contact have fewer allergies than urban children despite similar rates of infection.
options.C: Children who suffer more infectious illnesses in their first years of life develop fewer allergies than their rarely sick peers.
options.D: Allergic and autoimmune disease is more common in wealthy countries than in poorer ones.

16.stem: Based on Text 2, the scholars it describes would most likely characterize the praise described in Text 1 as one that

options.A: correctly locates the power of the lyrics in Wordsworth's unforced sincerity.
options.B: wrongly assumes that Wordsworth revised his finished lyrics far more heavily than he actually did.
options.C: understates how much genuine feeling survives into the finished lyrics.
options.D: mistakes a deliberately crafted impression of spontaneity for genuinely unmediated feeling.

17.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the chemist's claim?

options.A: At 10 C the salt dissolved to 21 g per 100 mL, the lowest value she recorded.
options.B: Solubility fell steadily as the temperature rose from 10 C to 70 C, ending at 21 g per 100 mL.
options.C: Solubility measured the same 39 g per 100 mL at both 30 C and 50 C.
options.D: As the temperature rose from 10 C to 70 C, solubility increased from 21 to 58 g per 100 mL.

18.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the ecologist's hypothesis?

options.A: Reefs with a greater variety of fish species also tended to recover more quickly once a bleaching event had passed.
options.B: Reefs sitting in cooler water bleached far less during the heat wave than reefs in the warmest parts of the same reef system.
options.C: During the heat wave, reefs hosting many algal strains lost far less living coral than nearby reefs hosting only one strain.
options.D: Corals can expel the algae they host and later take up new strains from the surrounding water once a bleaching event has ended.

19.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Medieval mountain villages were rarely abandoned for any reason other than a sudden and severe change in the local climate.
options.B: The village's residents were too poor to salvage the timber and iron fittings from their houses before they left the site.
options.C: A single harsh winter forced every household in the mountain village to abandon its houses at more or less the same moment.
options.D: Excavation evidence indicates the village was abandoned gradually and deliberately, not in a single catastrophe.

20.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to complete the text?

options.A: Program A's weakest school gained less than a tenth of what Program B's weakest school gained.
options.B: the highest gain recorded under Program A fell short of every gain recorded under Program B.
options.C: Program B's larger average gain rests on results from a quarter as many schools as Program A's does.
options.D: gains under Program B varied more widely across schools than gains under Program A did.

21.stem: Which choice best describes what the transplant experiments allow the botanists to conclude?

options.A: The difference in bloom timing arose from local growing conditions rather than from inherited traits.
options.B: Because both slopes shared the same final frost date, that date was the primary factor determining when each plant bloomed.
options.C: The windward and sheltered populations belonged to genetically distinct varieties.
options.D: Seedlings moved between slopes failed to survive in their new locations.

22.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the scientist's claim?

options.A: Bread stored at 20 C and bread stored at 10 C both lasted the same number of days before spoiling.
options.B: Bread stored at 30 C spoiled in 4 days.
options.C: Bread stored at 4 C, the lowest temperature, lasted 20 days, the longest of the four conditions.
options.D: Bread stored at the highest temperature lasted the longest.

23.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the passage's central qualification?

options.A: In regions with many internally cohesive but socially homogeneous associations, trust between different social groups was unusually low.
options.B: Regions with denser networks of clubs, choirs, and bowling leagues of every kind also recorded higher voter turnout.
options.C: Members of bowling leagues and choirs report trusting other members far more than they trust neighbors who belong to no association at all.
options.D: Larger civic associations tend to dissolve within a few years, while smaller clubs and choirs persist for decades.

24.stem: The passage is primarily structured to

options.A: demonstrate that placebo pills relieve chronic pain and irritable bowel syndrome about as effectively as active drugs do for those conditions.
options.B: argue that patients' expectations play no part in producing the relief that placebo pills deliver.
options.C: trace the development of open-label placebo research from its earliest trials to the present day.
options.D: challenge one specific assumption about the placebo effect while carefully bounding what the challenge does and does not establish.
